title: Care planning, comorbidity, evaluation and referral
blurb: Turn an assessment into a person-centred plan with agreed goals, prioritise when someone has several conditions, evaluate honestly and refer safely.
question: Mrs Nwosu, 76, has heart failure, type 2 diabetes, osteoarthritis and depression, and takes 11 regular medicines. She has fallen twice this year and has nine appointments this month. Her main wish is to attend her granddaughter's wedding in 6 weeks. How should the nurse approach her care plan?

teach.h: From assessment to a plan you agree together
teach.body: A care plan turns assessment findings into needs, goals, actions and a date to review. The NMC expects you to process assessment information into person-centred, evidence-based plans with agreed goals, to work in partnership to monitor and reassess them, and to know when and how to refer. Plain English: what matters to this person, what will we do about it, how will we know it has worked, and who else needs to help?
teach.cite: NMC proficiencies P3.5, P3.15, P3.16; Code 2.1, 3.3

teach.caption: The plan is never finished: evaluation feeds straight back into assessment, and goals are readjusted and progress documented (P3.15).

teach.body: A good goal is the person's own, written so anyone can tell whether it has been met: what they will do, how much, with what help, and by when. The Code asks you to work in partnership, to encourage and empower people to share decisions, and to respect how far they want to be involved. A goal the nurse sets alone, such as 'improve mobility', cannot be evaluated and may not matter to the person.

rows.label: Mobility
values: Walk 30 m with frame and 1 helper by Friday

rows.label: Pain
values: Pain 3/10 or less when walking, by day 3

teach.h: When to take account of multimorbidity (NICE NG56 rec 1.2.1)
head: Consider this approach if the person...
rows: Finds it hard to manage treatments or daily activities
Receives care from several services and needs more
Has both long-term physical and mental health conditions
Often seeks unplanned or emergency care
teach.caption: Or if the person asks for it. Comorbidity changes priorities: treatments for one condition can harm another or add to the burden.

teach.h: An approach that takes account of multimorbidity (NG56 rec 1.5.2)

steps.label: Goals, values, priorities
steps.sub: What matters most to the person

steps.label: Review treatments
steps.sub: Benefits and harms for this person

teach.body: Evaluation compares where the person is now with the goal you agreed: met, partly met or not met, and why. Record it at the time or as soon as possible, attributed to you, dated and timed, without unnecessary abbreviations, jargon or speculation, and note any risks and the steps taken (Code 10.1–10.4). If a goal is not met, reassess with the person and revise the plan rather than simply rolling it forward.

children.label: Ask a suitably qualified professional for help

teach.caption: Explain the referral and agree it with the person; state the reason, urgency and relevant findings; keep colleagues informed when sharing care (Code 8.3); document it.

teach.h: Worked example: Mrs Nwosu, district nursing caseload
items: Assess: two falls, breathless on stairs, low mood, 11 medicines, nine appointments in four places this month.
Priorities: she wants to attend the wedding in 6 weeks; together they agree 'walk from the car to the venue with her stick, without a fall'.
Burden: she finds the appointments exhausting, so the nurse explores combining them and asks the GP for a medicines review, given her falls.
Refer: physiotherapy for strength and balance; lying and standing BP shared with the GP.
Plan: one named coordinator, review in 1 week, how to get urgent help. Evaluate at each visit and readjust.

teach.text: Following every single-condition guideline for someone with five conditions can do more harm than good: NICE NG56 asks you to weigh benefits and risks for the individual and their priorities. And evaluation is not 'care given as planned': it is whether the goal was achieved.

items: Assess, agree goals, plan, implement, evaluate, reassess: a cycle, not a form.
Goals are the person's own, measurable and timed.
Multimorbidity (NG56): establish disease and treatment burden and priorities, review treatments, agree one plan with a coordinator.
Document evaluation at the time: dated, timed, attributed, no speculation (Code 10).
Ask for help beyond your competence (13.3); make timely referrals (13.2) with the person's agreement.

summary: You can now build a person-centred care plan with measurable, agreed goals, prioritise when someone lives with several conditions using NICE NG56, and evaluate and document progress honestly. You know when to ask for help and how to refer safely.

A.q: Mr Dunn, 68, had a knee replacement and wants to get back to his allotment. Which goal is best written for his care plan?
options: Mr Dunn will walk 50 m with one stick by Friday
Nurses will encourage Mr Dunn to mobilise more often
Mr Dunn will improve his mobility as soon as possible
Mr Dunn will be independent in all daily activities
A.why: This goal is the person's, measurable (50 m, one stick) and timed (by Friday), so it can be evaluated and links to what matters to him.

whyNot.1: This describes a nursing action, not the outcome Mr Dunn will achieve.
whyNot.2: 'Improve' and 'as soon as possible' cannot be measured or evaluated.
whyNot.3: 'All daily activities' is too broad and has no measure or date.

A.q: A nurse compares Mrs Kaur's pain score today with the goal agreed yesterday and records whether it was met. Which stage of care planning is this?
options: Assessment
Planning
Implementation
Evaluation
A.why: Evaluation measures progress against the agreed goal and leads to reassessment and readjustment (P3.15).

whyNot.0: Assessment gathers information to identify needs; this nurse is measuring against a goal already set.
whyNot.1: Planning sets goals and actions; here the goal already exists.
whyNot.2: Implementation is delivering the care, not judging whether the goal was met.

A.q: A community nurse finds that Mrs Bell's leg wound has features she has not been trained to manage. What does the NMC Code require?
options: Ask a suitably qualified professional for help
Continue the current plan and review in a month
Try a new dressing she has read about online
Ask Mrs Bell's family to keep an eye on it
A.why: Code 13.3: ask for help from a suitably qualified and experienced professional to carry out any action or procedure beyond the limits of your competence.

whyNot.1: Continuing an unsuitable plan delays the expertise the wound needs.
whyNot.2: Trying an unfamiliar treatment is acting beyond competence, which the Code forbids.
whyNot.3: Family monitoring does not replace professional assessment.

B.q: Which person most clearly meets NICE NG56 criteria for an approach to care that takes account of multimorbidity?
options: Mr Ali, 58, hypertension controlled on one tablet
Mrs Nwosu, 76, heart failure, depression and falls
Ms Fry, 45, asthma and a recently sprained ankle
Mr Cole, 62, type 2 diabetes managed by diet
B.why: NG56 rec 1.2.1 includes having both long-term physical and mental health conditions, and having frailty or falls; Mrs Nwosu has both.

whyNot.0: One well-controlled condition with a single medicine does not meet the NG56 criteria.
whyNot.2: A short-term injury alongside asthma does not by itself meet the criteria.
whyNot.3: A single long-term condition managed by diet does not meet the criteria.

B.q: Which evaluation entry best meets the NMC Code on records?
options: 16/03 Walked well with frame today, goal nearly met. K Obi
16/03 15:10 Seems unmotivated, refused walk, ?depressed. K Obi RN
16/03 15:10 Walked 20 m, frame, 1 helper (goal 30 m by Fri). K Obi RN
Mobilised as per care plan today. Will review again later. KO
B.why: Code 10: entries are dated, timed and attributed, and should identify progress clearly. This entry measures progress against the goal and is signed.

whyNot.0: It has no time and gives no measure of progress against the goal; 'walked well' cannot be evaluated.
whyNot.1: It contains speculation and judgement, which Code 10.4 says to avoid.
whyNot.3: It records an action, not the outcome, and has no date, time or full signature.

B.q: Mrs Nwosu says she has nine appointments this month in four places and feels exhausted. Under NICE NG56, what should the nurse explore with her?
options: Adding a clinic to monitor her fatigue
Ways to coordinate or reduce her appointments
Why each appointment is essential for her
Raising the dose of her antidepressant
B.why: NG56 asks clinicians to establish treatment burden, including the number and place of appointments, and to look for alternative follow-up arrangements to coordinate or optimise them.

whyNot.0: Another appointment adds to the burden she has described.
whyNot.2: Justifying every appointment does not address the burden or her quality of life.
whyNot.3: Her exhaustion is linked to appointments; changing medicines is not the first step NG56 describes.

C.q: Mrs Nwosu is offered a new diuretic. She declines, because frequent urination would stop her attending her granddaughter's wedding next month. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Insist that she takes it as the guideline recommends
Ask her daughter to persuade her to take it after all
Record her refusal in the notes and take no further action
Weigh risks and benefits with her, around her priorities
C.why: NG56 rec 1.1.4: weigh the benefits and risks of single-condition treatments and discuss them alongside the person's preferences. Code 2.5: respect and document the right to accept or refuse treatment.

whyNot.0: Insisting ignores her right to decide and the NG56 approach to multimorbidity.
whyNot.1: Using family to pressure her undermines her autonomy.
whyNot.2: Recording a refusal without exploring options leaves her heart failure unaddressed.

C.q: Mr Dunn's goal was to walk 50 m with one stick by Friday. On Friday he manages 15 m, limited by knee pain. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Keep the same goal and extend it by one week
Reassess with him, explore why and revise the plan
Mark it achieved because he tried very hard
Close the care plan as he is due home
C.why: When a goal is not met, evaluation should lead to reassessment with the person (here, of his pain), readjusted goals and documented progress (P3.15).

whyNot.0: Extending the date without addressing the pain repeats the same plan with the same result.
whyNot.2: Effort is not achievement; marking it met is inaccurate recording.
whyNot.3: An unmet goal and uncontrolled pain need action, not closure.

C.q: Mrs Nwosu sees cardiology, the diabetes team, her GP and the district nurses. To reduce duplication, what should her individualised management plan include under NICE NG56?
options: A separate plan from each specialist team
Weekly hospital reviews by each specialist
Who is responsible for coordinating her care
Her full medical history written out in detail
C.why: NG56 rec 1.5.2: the agreed plan includes who is responsible for coordination of care and how the plan is communicated to all professionals and services involved.

whyNot.0: Separate plans are the fragmentation NG56 aims to reduce.
whyNot.3: A detailed history does not establish who coordinates care.

reteach.title: Four questions on a single page
reteach.question: Strip a care plan back to its bones. Which four questions must it answer?

blocks.h: What, how, how will we know, who else?
blocks.body: What matters to this person and what is the need? How will we meet it? How will we know it worked (a measure and a date)? Who else needs to help (a referral, a coordinator)? If your plan answers those four, agreed with the person and written so a colleague can pick it up, it is a care plan.

blocks.h: A care plan in four words

blocks.text: 'Care given as planned' is implementation, not evaluation. Evaluation asks whether the goal was achieved, and what to change if not.

explain.body: Assess, identify needs, agree goals and plan, implement, evaluate, reassess. Evaluation feeds back into the next assessment.

test.q: Agreeing goals with a person and deciding the actions to reach them happens in which stage?
options: Evaluation
Assessment
Planning
Implementation
test.why: Planning sets the agreed goals and the actions to achieve them.

whyNot.0: Evaluation measures whether goals were met.
whyNot.1: Assessment gathers the information that identifies needs.
whyNot.3: Implementation carries out the planned actions.

explain.body: The person's own priority, stating what they will achieve, how much, with what help and by when, so anyone can evaluate it.

test.q: Which feature most makes a care plan goal possible to evaluate?
options: A list of the nursing actions
A measurable outcome and a date
The diagnosis written in full
The signature of the ward manager
test.why: A measurable outcome and a timescale let anyone judge whether the goal has been met.

whyNot.0: Actions describe what staff do, not what the person achieves.
whyNot.2: The diagnosis gives context but not a measure of progress.
whyNot.3: A manager's signature does not make a goal measurable.

explain.body: NICE NG56 focuses on how conditions and treatments interact, the person's priorities, and reducing treatment burden, adverse events and unplanned care, with better coordination.

test.q: According to NICE NG56, what is the purpose of an approach to care that takes account of multimorbidity?
options: To follow every single-condition guideline
To transfer care to one specialist team
To improve quality of life
To reduce the number of diagnoses made
test.why: NG56 rec 1.6.2: discuss with the person that the purpose is to improve quality of life, for example by reducing treatment burden and optimising care.

whyNot.0: Following every single-condition guideline can increase burden and harm.
whyNot.1: NG56 aims to coordinate care across services, not hand it all to one specialist.
whyNot.3: The aim concerns quality of life, not the number of diagnoses.

explain.body: Make a timely referral when care or treatment from another practitioner is needed (Code 13.2). Explain it to the person and agree it, give the reason, urgency and relevant findings, keep colleagues informed and document it.

test.q: Under the NMC Code, when should a nurse refer a person to another practitioner?
options: In a timely way, when care from them is needed
Once the person has asked for the referral twice
At the next multidisciplinary meeting
After the current plan has run for a month
test.why: Code 13.2: make a timely referral to another practitioner when any action, care or treatment is required.

whyNot.1: Referral is based on need, not on the number of requests.
whyNot.2: Waiting for a meeting may delay care that is needed now.
whyNot.3: A fixed waiting period is not a reason to delay a needed referral.
